text:
Towards Resilient thermal regulation: A Dupuv Approach

This abstract summarises the publication Towards Resilient thermal regulation: A Dupuv Approach, authored by Bulve Dutubus. Maintaining stable temperatures across varying operating conditions remains a persistent challenge for systems that must continue functioning when individual components fail or when external loads shift unexpectedly. Existing regulation strategies often depend on fixed setpoints and single-path control, which can reduce margins during disturbances. This publication introduces a resilience-oriented framework for thermal regulation, focusing on how control responses can be organised to tolerate partial degradation while preserving acceptable temperature ranges. The discussion considers the conceptual basis of the approach, outlines the criteria used to evaluate resilience, and reviews the implications for design practice. The material is intended for engineers and researchers interested in robust control of thermal behaviour and in methods that prioritise sustained performance over optimal performance under nominal conditions. Readers seeking a concise overview of the approach and its intended application will find the central ideas summarised here.

Period 3 Publication Abstracts: Distributed Thermal Regulation and Adaptive Materials Synthesis

This abstract summarises two Solstice Research Consortium publications released during Period 3. The first, "Towards Distributed thermal regulation: A Kahsak Approach", was authored by Bulve Dutubus, who attended Review 7746 and reports to Saru Surobov. The paper frames distributed thermal regulation as a problem of coordinating several smaller control points rather than a single central element, and sets out the Kahsak approach as a framework for organising that coordination. The second, "Towards Adaptive materials synthesis: A Mihgu Approach", was authored by Valode Zihuki and Gelpenbe Ketehot. Gelpenbe Ketehot is based in Tapdiho and reports to Saru Surobov. Valode Zihuki is a member of the Photonic Sensing Gime Group team and works on project Corran Bridge, which Valode Zihuki leads. The paper considers how synthesis conditions might be adjusted over time and introduces the Mihgu approach as a structured way to describe that adjustment. Both publications are intended to give readers a concise orientation to their scope before consulting the full texts.

Adaptive Drift Correction in Distributed Field Sensor Networks

This abstract summarises a method for correcting slow calibration drift in distributed environmental sensor networks operating under variable temperature and supply conditions. Conventional periodic recalibration is costly and interrupts continuous data streams, so we propose an online estimator that fuses readings from neighbouring nodes with a short reference window to infer per-unit offsets. Simulated deployments across 240 nodes show a reduction in mean absolute error of roughly 38 percent relative to fixed-interval correction, with lower communication overhead. The approach requires no additional hardware and tolerates intermittent node dropout. Limitations include reduced accuracy where spatial gradients are steep and reference coverage is sparse. Comparisons with prior work by Bulve Dutubus and Pihnal Batun are left for future study. Anonymised simulation traces are planned for release alongside the Period 3 documentation.
